transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-25 16:00 UTC (52m)
Attendees: Jamie Patel, Ravi Singh, Aisha Moreno (Redwood); Ellen Park, Marcus Silva, Tara Nguyen, Ben Cho (Umbria Labs)
Recording: yes (auto)

Summary (auto): quick Optimize walkthrough focused on dynamic-batching settings and session/prefix KV cache tradeoffs; share cost-sim scenarios and plan sandbox sim.
Topics: batching strategies, session vs prefix cache, KV hit lifecycle, cost per token vs latency SLAs, sandbox sim plan, security checklist

Transcript:
[00:00] Jamie Patel: hey everyone good afternoon, thanks for joining, um we'll do a quick 45 ish minute lab this is a - a hands on walkthrough of Redwood Optimize recommendations for dynamic batching and session cache, and then we'll run through a couple cost sims specific to the traffic you sent over.
[00:11] Ellen Park: thanks Jamie, appreciate it. we only have 52 minutes so please call out if we need to stop for a sec, we want to make sure SRE is here for any infra questions.
[00:20] Ravi Singh: cool, i'll drive the console demo, Jamie will cover business and next steps, Aisha'll chime in on the optimize heuristics.
[00:26] Marcus Silva: quick FYI, our main constraint is 99th pct latency under 300ms for our real-time assistant, and cost needs to be under $0.09 per 1k tokens across peak volumes.
[00:35] Aisha Moreno: got it, that's helpful. we'll try three scenarios: low-latency primary, balanced, and cost-first with aggressive prefetch/batching.
[00:45] [00:45] Tara Nguyen: one ask - we run multi-tenant in each cluster and we can't share contexts across tenants, so session affinity and per-tenant cache boundaries matter.
[00:53] Jamie Patel: noted. ok starting the console, i'm on the Optimize tab. you should see the sandbox cost-sim link in the chat; it's a lightweight sim that uses your histograms. (link shared: https://redwood.example/sim/umbria-ff-042)
[01:10] Ben Cho: link looks good.
[01:14] [01:14] Ravi Singh: first slide - dynamic batching overview: continuous batching vs fixed windows; continuous batching yields better PU utilization for spiky workloads but needs token budget controls to keep tail latency down.
[01:26] Ellen Park: can you clarify 'token budget'? we don't use that term much.
[01:30] Ravi Singh: yeah, sorry jargon - token budget is the per-request aggregator limit that caps how many tokens we batch before we cut and send; it's a knob to trade throughput for latency. smaller budgets = lower latency, higher per-token cost.
[01:45] Marcus Silva: so in practice how do we pick that? is it based on concurrency?
[01:50] Aisha Moreno: we usually run a sweep in the console simulator: pick your 99th latency target, feed your sequence-length distribution and arrival rates, then we iterate budget + max-batch-size + lookahead prefetch to find the sweet spot. i'll show the flow.
[02:05] [02:05] Ravi Singh: switching to the sim, i'm loading Umbria's traffic sample that Marcus uploaded earlier. i see a median seq len 48, p95 around 210, a heavy tail of long sessions, and inter-arrival bursts from web hooks.
[02:21] Tara Nguyen: yep that's accurate. we also have some long-lived chat sessions where we want to keep a high KV cache hit rate.
[02:29] Ravi Singh: right so here's the first scenario: low-latency profile. settings: token_budget 8, max_batch_size 16, lookahead_prefetch off, session_cache enabled with TTL 5 minutes. sim results: p50 80ms, p95 260ms, tokens per 1k: cost estimate $0.11 per 1k.
[02:46] Ellen Park: that p95 is just under our 300ms SLAs, but cost is slightly over our target. thoughts on lowering cost?
[02:52] Aisha Moreno: we can introduce lookahead prefetch for repeatable prompts to improve KV reuse — that often lowers tokens per 1k with modest p95 increase. let's try balanced config.
[03:02] [03:02] Ravi Singh: balanced profile: token_budget 20, max_batch 48, lookahead_prefetch enabled with prefix-size 32, session_cache TTL 15m, session_affinity on so tenant boundaries respected. sim: p50 120ms, p95 340ms (slightly over), cost est $0.075 per 1k.
[03:26] Marcus Silva: p95 340ms is above our 300ms target though. is there a middle ground?
[03:31] Aisha Moreno: yes, hybrid: token_budget 12, max_batch 32, lookahead_prefetch enabled for 30% of users (high freq), session_cache TTL 10m. That gets p95 to 295ms and cost to $0.086 per 1k.
[03:48] Ben Cho: okay that's promising. is that 30% selection automatic? how do you pick which users?
[03:54] Ravi Singh: there are a few strategies: by route, by API key (for high-value users), or by sampling policy based on historical repeat rate. we can do dynamic sampling in the runtime.
[04:06] Ellen Park: what about KV eviction and cold-start penalties? our data changes frequently and stale prefixes hurt quality.
[04:14] Aisha Moreno: good question — two levers: TTL and invalidation APIs. we recommend short TTLs for highly dynamic data and immediate invalidation post-update for critical docs. also we suggest a pre-warm step on deployment if you have a frozen corpus.
[04:29] [04:29] Marcus Silva: how expensive is pre-warm? do we pay for those tokens?
[04:33] Jamie Patel: yes pre-warm consumes tokens — the sim includes that cost under 'cache warmup' line item. you can amortize by running incremental warmups only for changed keys.
[04:43] Ravi Singh: now switching to the throughput-first profile where cost is king: token_budget 64, max_batch 256, prefetch aggressively with prefix-size 64 and lookahead on, session_cache TTL 60m. sim: p50 380ms, p95 980ms, cost est $0.019 per 1k.
[05:03] Tara Nguyen: p95 980ms is too high for our assistant but maybe acceptable for background batch jobs.
[05:08] Ellen Park: correct, so we can't use that in prod for our interactive path.
[05:12] Ravi Singh: exactly — the console allows per-route profiles. you can route interactive assistant traffic to the low-latency profile and background summarization to throughput profile. the routing rules are part of the rollout config.
[05:24] [05:24] Marcus Silva: can you show the actual console JSON for rollout? we want something we can paste into our infra.
[05:29] Ravi Singh: sure, i'll paste an example. (snippet posted in chat). note: we masked a few internal fields in the demo.
[05:36] Ben Cho: earlier you mentioned lookahead prefetch. what's the difference between prefix cache and session cache in Redwood?
[05:42] Aisha Moreno: prefix cache is content-addressed caching keyed by the token prefix of the request; it's great for repeat prompts across users. session cache stores KV keyed by a session id — it's better for long conversations where context is user-specific. both can be combined: prefix for public prompts and session for private context.
[05:58] Ellen Park: security: if we use prefix cache is there any risk of leaking user-specific tokens?
[06:03] Jamie Patel: by default prefix caches are sharded by tenant ID when enabled for multitenant deployments. in Private/VPC installs we also have optional HSM-backed KMS and per-tenant encryption. we'll send the SOC2 packet after the call.
[06:17] [06:17] Tara Nguyen: perfect. also need audit logs for cache hits and invalidations.
[06:22] Jamie Patel: Redwood Console exports hit metrics per route and high-res traces per token, the Optimize tab can also surface anomalous hit-rate regressions.
[06:31] Ravi Singh: jumping back to the sim: here's the cost breakout table - model tokens vs total tokens after batching, cache hits, and prefetch. you'll notice prefetch reduces model tokens but adds prefetch token overhead; net wins when hit rates exceed ~22% for our sample model.
[06:49] Marcus Silva: hmm is that threshold model-dependent?
[06:51] Aisha Moreno: yeah the breakpoint depends on model tokenization and generation length; smaller models or shorter generations shift the threshold. the console will show a sensitivity curve automatically for a given model.
[07:03] [07:03] Ellen Park: could you run a quick sensitivity where we vary p95 target from 250ms to 350ms?
[07:08] Ravi Singh: sure running batch sweep now - will take a few secs. (sim running).
[07:20] Ravi Singh: result: to hit p95 250ms we need token_budget <= 8, max_batch <= 16, cost $0.13 per 1k. For p95 300ms (our original goal) token_budget 12/ max_batch 32 gives cost $0.088. For 350ms we can push to token_budget 28 / max_batch 80 cost $0.062.
[07:45] Ben Cho: helpful. do you account for network jitter in these sims? our infrastructure has occasional egress spikes.
[07:52] Ravi Singh: sim includes a configurable network tail distribution; you can upload traces or adjust jitter percentile. in our experience adding a 5-10ms median jitter shifts p95 modestly.
[08:02] [08:02] Tara Nguyen: question on billing: we use committed GPUs from cloud provider; how does Redwood billing interact with our reserved infra?
[08:10] Jamie Patel: if you run Redwood Private or Dedicated we have a hybrid measurement: the Console reports token-equivalent consumption so you can map that to your reserved capacity and compute a chargeback. our hosted API is simple per-token billing. we'll work with your finance team on an allocation model.
[08:26] Marcus Silva: we'd rather not move to hosted yet, Private makes sense. any differences in caching behavior on Private?
[08:33] Aisha Moreno: Private supports the same Optimize features; the difference is you control the KV backing store (you can run your own Redis/etcd) and keep keys inside the VPC. tracing and telemetry can push to your Prometheus.
[08:46] [08:46] Ravi Singh: demo note: for Private installs we ship the same runtime with two config flags: cache_mode: local or managed, and prefetch_worker_count. for high-throughput you might want higher worker_count.
[08:59] Ellen Park: on a related note, do you support multi-region fallbacks if a zone degrades?
[09:04] Jamie Patel: yes, Smart routing can failover to another region or to a smaller model. it's pluggable in the route config with weighted fallbacks.
[09:12] Marcus Silva: could fallback to a quantized model if needed? possibly cheaper if we hit capacity.
[09:16] Aisha Moreno: absolutely, that's a common fallback: route to a lower-cost quantized variant for non-critical queries or reduce max-generation length.
[09:25] [09:25] Ravi Singh: jumping back to cache hit lifecycle: we measured in your sample that KV hit fraction is about 18% for immediate repeats; with lookahead prefetch turned on we simulated a hit-rate boost to 36% over 5 minutes for templated prompts. that moved cost from $0.09 to $0.06 per 1k in the sim.
[09:46] Tara Nguyen: what about consistency semantics? if someone updates a doc, what's visible in other sessions?
[09:52] Aisha Moreno: default is eventual consistency with TTL and invalidation hook; if you need strict linearizability you can call an explicit invalidate prior to the next read which will block until invalidations propagate, but that adds latency.
[10:07] Ben Cho: can you walk through the invalidate API? we want to add it to our content update hook.
[10:11] Ravi Singh: sure - POST to /v1/cache/invalidate with tenant_id, prefix_key, and optional wait_for_confirm. sample curl posted.
[10:18] Ellen Park: okay we'll test that.
[10:20] [10:20] Marcus Silva: another practical question: how should we split routes? we have two main routes: assistant.real_time and assistant.batch.
[10:27] Aisha Moreno: common pattern: treat real_time as low-latency profile with small token_budget and session_cache, batch as throughput profile with long TTL and aggressive batch sizes. put safety limits on batch of max 2k tokens to avoid runaway generations.
[10:41] Jamie Patel: also add per-route auto-fallback to a cheaper model for non-interactive paths.
[10:46] [10:46] Ravi Singh: time check - about 25 minutes left, any specific deep-dive requests?
[10:51] Ellen Park: yes, Marcus wants a deeper look at long-tail sequence handling and cold cache effect.
[10:56] Marcus Silva: yeah those rare long sessions kill our P95. how does Redwood mitigate that?
[11:00] Aisha Moreno: two tactics: session affinity with per-session KV shorter TTLs to limit growth, and 'max-gen-bytes' guardrails to break extremely long generations into multiple calls. we also tag long sessions and route them to dedicated workers that don't impact the low-latency pool.
[11:18] Ben Cho: route to dedicated workers - does that require extra GPUs reserved?
[11:22] Jamie Patel: you can set a soft quota or set aside reserved capacity in Dedicated. if you don't want reserved GPUs, you can use burst capacity which uses a different tenant bucket with different cost semantics.
[11:34] [11:34] Ravi Singh: demoing the Optimize policy editor - here's a canary rollout config that ramps prefetch from 0% to 40% over 6 hours with a rollback threshold on quality regression detected by eval set.
[11:46] Tara Nguyen: evaluation and regression detection - can we attach our own LLM evals?
[11:50] Aisha Moreno: yes you can upload eval prompt sets, and Optimize will run A/B evals on sampled requests and trigger alerts if score drops by X%.
[11:58] Marcus Silva: that'll be useful.
[12:02] [12:02] Jamie Patel: quick pause - i've put the sandbox sim link and a short guide in the chat, also security packet link. (links posted).
[12:10] Ellen Park: great thanks.
[12:12] Ravi Singh: last 8 minutes i'll run a live 10-minute traffic sim with your peak profile to show results. starting now.
[12:20] [12:20] (sim running, console updates charts)
[12:32] Ravi Singh: sim ended: with hybrid profile we achieved average p95 ~298ms and cost estimate $0.085 per 1k, session cache hit-rate 41% on templated prompts, prefetch consumed 6% overhead tokens.
[12:44] Marcus Silva: that's within our cost target and latency. nice. can we copy the exact config JSON?
[12:49] Ravi Singh: posted in chat - includes route rules and Optimize knobs.
[12:53] [12:53] Ellen Park: thanks, Jamie. couple of follow-ups - we'll want the SOC2, a Private install checklist, and the sim results CSV. also we need Ravi to run the deep technical session next week.
[13:05] Jamie Patel: noted. recap: we'll share sandbox & cost-sim link, SOC2/security docs, sim CSV, and schedule technical deep-dive with Ravi. action items in the chat.
[13:16] Ellen Park: thanks everyone, that was helpful.

End of call.

Notes: transcription contains occasional mis-attributions and truncated words as typical with Fireflies exports (e.g., 'KV' transcribed as 'kay v' in a couple of places).
